title: Revoking the token didn’t kill the backdoor
raw_text: Every identity-compromise runbook I have written, read or inherited has the same step near the top: revoke the tokens. Reset the password, kill the sessions, invalidate the refresh tokens, then go hunting. It is the right instinct. Against adversary-in-the-middle phishing, where the whole prize is a stolen session cookie, revocation is the move that ends the incident. Then I spent a few days taking apart a backdoor where that step buys you nothing at all. The reason sits in one function, and it is the last place most of us would think to look. The sample is GraphWorm, a custom implant tied to the China-nexus APT group Webworm. One thing I found there rewrote a line in my own incident response procedure, and I think it belongs in yours. The C2 channel is somebody’s OneDrive GraphWorm has no C2 domain, no beacon to a rented VPS, no hardcoded address to block. It authenticates to Microsoft Graph as an OAuth application and uses a OneDrive account as a dead drop. The layout is simple enough to sketch on a napkin. The operator writes an encrypted task file into a job folder. The implant polls that folder, runs the task, then uploads the encrypted result into a result folder. A heartbeat file gets a fresh timestamp every interval and a fingerprint file carries the victim’s system details. The command set covers shell execution, file upload and download, sleep, kill and a key exchange pair that upgrades the deployment key to per-session keys. All of it rides graph.microsoft.com over TLS, from a host that is already talking to Microsoft 365 all day. There is no unusual destination for a firewall to flag, no freshly registered domain for a reputation engine to penalize, no odd port. The network layer has nothing to say. That is the design goal, and it is the same shift I have written about before, where operators stop building their own infrastructure and start running on somebody else’s . The credentials are all sitting in the binary in cleartext: a client ID, a client secret, a tenant ID and a refresh token more than 1,300 characters long. The operator also shipped a debug build with the full PDB path intact. One more detail matters for anyone planning a response. The implant does not identify its victims by hostname or address. It builds an identifier by hashing the network adapter’s hardware address together with CPU and disk serial numbers pulled through WMI. Rename the machine, move it to a different subnet or put it behind a new egress address, and the operator still recognizes it as the same box. Any containment plan that leans on changing the victim’s network identity is solving a problem this implant does not have. So far this is a good story but a familiar one. Cloud-hosted C2 is not new. The part I did not expect was in the tasking handler. The function that breaks the runbook Among the commands the implant accepts is one called upgrade. The flow is short, and it is worth walking through. The handler parses a configuration blob out of the incoming task. It then destroys all five credential strings held in the beacon object, copies five new ones in, rebuilds the OAuth scope structure, tests a connection against the new OneDrive account, writes the replacement configuration to disk and swaps the live API instance. One task. Entire identity replaced. Sit with the consequence for a second. Your investigation reaches the point where you have identified the application, you file with the platform and the tokens get revoked. The implant’s next poll fails. If the operator is watching, and an operator writing a heartbeat file every interval is watching, they queue an upgrade task pointing at a second OneDrive account they registered months ago. The implant collects it, rotates and resumes. Nothing on the endpoint changed. No new binary, no new persistence mechanism, no new process. Same file on disk, different identity behind it. Revocation removed a credential. It did not remove access. This does not appear in the public reporting on the family, which is not a criticism. Vendor writeups are scoped to the campaign they observed, and this is the kind of detail you only see with the decompiler open on a function nobody had a reason to prioritize. I confirmed it twice before I was willing to write it down, once from the extracted strings and once from the decompiled function itself. The credential field offsets I recovered from the strings had to line up with the offsets the constructor actually reads from, and they did, which is the difference between a finding and a guess. What I changed afterward Three things came out of this that I would put into an identity response procedure tomorrow. Treat revocation as a delay rather than an eviction whenever the C2 rides an application identity . The durable object is the registration, not the tokens it issues. Tokens are leaves, the registration is the root, and containment that stops at revoking has started a timer rather than closed a door. If the registration lives in a tenant, you do not control, suspension means filing a report and waiting on somebody else’s queue, so file early rather than as a last step. Assume the operator holds a spare. Credential rotation costs an attacker almost nothing and costs you an entire response cycle. That asymmetry should drive sequencing: remove the endpoint’s ability to reach the channel at the same moment you burn the credential, not afterward. Isolating the host, or blocking that specific application from authenticating in your own tenant, are both moves that do not depend on anyone else’s cooperation. Hunt on the identity plane, because the network plane is blind here. The detections that actually fire on this family are not network signatures at all. They are cloud telemetry queries: the operator’s application ID appearing in your sign-in events, authentication against an unfamiliar tenant, a non-browser HTTP library user agent hitting OneDrive, the beacon and fingerprint file names showing up in file telemetry. The application ID is a fixed string; it belongs to nobody legitimate, and a single query across your sign-in telemetry answers whether it has ever asked your tenant for a token. None of that needs new tooling. It needs the application registration treated as the thing you are trying to kill. The wider pattern is what stayed with me. We spent a decade learning to hunt infrastructure, and adversaries answered by not having any. When the channel is a folder in a cloud tenant, and the identity behind that folder can be swapped by remote command, the artifacts we are trained to chase are precisely the ones an operator can replace most cheaply. What they cannot replace cheaply is the code sitting on the endpoint and the behavior of that code inside your telemetry. So, I check the assumption now. Before calling an identity incident contained, I ask what specifically I killed, and whether the adversary can hand themselves a replacement without ever touching the victim’s machine. In this sample, the answer was yes, and it took one function to prove it. The full teardown and detection content from this analysis are published on GitHub .

title: 5 ways AI is reshaping the cybersecurity job market
raw_text: Mario Platt spent part of last year eliminating a team. As CISO for online password management service LastPass, he shut down the company’s dedicated vulnerability management function in late 2025, folding its responsibilities directly into IT and product security. AI and business intelligence tools now handle the triage and analysis that once required a standing group of specialists. It’s a concrete example of a trend that’s largely lived in the abstract: security work reorganizing itself around what AI can now do faster than people can. The pressure to rethink cybersecurity roles for this new era is profound: 87% of organizations cite AI-related vulnerabilities as their fastest-growing risk category, according to the World Economic Forum’s 2026 Global Cybersecurity Outlook . Companies are already responding. The 2026 SANS/GIAC Cybersecurity Workforce Research Report found that 74% of organizations say AI is already affecting the size of their security teams and the shape of the roles within them. Ask security leaders and staffing experts whether AI is creating new jobs, killing old ones, or just changing what the people already there do, and they’ll tell you it’s a bit of each. Here are five ways that’s playing out across companies. 1. Security leadership is consolidating, not multiplying Some cyber roles were eliminated alongside consolidation at LastPass. Platt is also partway through a similar shakeup in his governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) function, automating the routine compliance work so the group can take on a higher-level risk advisory role, with staff evolving into full business information security officers aligned to specific business units. Elsewhere, entire functions are consolidating under one executive rather than splitting up among new ones. Burke Autrey, president of technology consulting and executive services firm Fortium Partners, says his firm’s standard advice to clients wrestling with AI governance comes down to one simple rule: Don’t invent another C-level title. One client recently consolidated infrastructure, information security, and AI/ML under an existing senior technology leader and promoted that person rather than recruiting a separate CISO and AI leader. Martha Heller, founder and CEO of executive search firm Heller, sees the same pattern in her practice. Clients increasingly want a single leader to run both infrastructure and cyber — particularly candidates who cut their teeth on a cloud migration. “Anybody who’s led a really successful cloud migration will know a thing or two about cyber,” she says. Most companies are still in an earlier, messier phase: piling AI governance duties onto existing security and privacy leaders without adding staff to match, says John Alford, CSO at Quant, where he leads security, compliance, and AI governance for the company’s agentic AI platform. “Companies will eventually formalize these responsibilities,” Alford says. “The current model puts too much risk into too few roles.” 2. The security analyst’s job is changing from finding answers to evaluating them At Nexus Black, the AI accelerator unit within enterprise software company IFS, head of cybersecurity Robin Fewster built an automation that scans security sources daily, checks affected packages against the company’s source code, and flags exposure. That kind of capability, he says, is becoming the baseline expectation rather than a specialty. And the line between security analyst and security engineer, Fewster says, is blurring. Detection tools already handle the who, what, when, and where of an incident quite well, says Randy Gross, CISO at CompTIA; the SOC analyst’s real value now is in answering the why. “‘Why’ unlocks business impact, appropriate response, and long-term mitigations,” Gross says, “and, as a bonus, it’s also moving some senior InfoSec functions left.” That doesn’t necessarily equate to fewer jobs, though. Automating a process or enriching telemetry won’t eliminate the person who did it, says Gross; it clears space to deal with GRC debt, incident response planning, and the rest of the backlog every security team has. Today’s analysts spend less time working the queue and more time designing, tuning, and validating the systems that work the queue, says Autrey of Fortium Partners. That evolution is producing new titles that didn’t exist 18 months ago, says Heller, including one companies are now asking for by name: agent security engineer. 3. Judgment, not technical knowledge, is the scarcest skill Judgment is “the hardest trait to hire for,” says Quant’s Alford. AI can produce a technically polished answer that ignores business impact or architecture, he says, and reduced cyber staffing leaves fewer experienced people around to catch it. Gross of CompTIA frames what’s happening in cyber hiring as a value shift: judgment, he says, is now in high demand. But it may also be in short supply, according to Autrey. Verifying an automated conclusion “takes more seniority than producing the finding ever did,” he says, “and that is the seat almost nobody has staffed.” That shortage is most acute for identity engineers and identity and access management (IAM) architects who understand machine and agent identity, a specialty nearly every client asks for and almost none can find, Autrey says. The mechanical work of parsing logs, correlating alerts, and first-pass triage has mostly moved to the model, says Rob T. Lee, chief AI officer and chief of research at SANS Institute. “What is left is judgment: knowing when the output is wrong, what to ask next, when to stop and escalate.” The problems compound when AI starts checking AI. Alford calls it the “AI loop”: one system drafts a policy or control, a second evaluates it, and a third produces the risk rating an executive actually sees — each layer potentially reinforcing the assumptions of the one before it. “The final report can look sophisticated even when the original assumption was wrong,” Alford says. Automation, he warns, “can fail confidently and at machine speed.” Breaking that loop still requires an experienced person to check the output against the actual architecture and business impact. 4. AI fluency has become a baseline hiring filter The share of cybersecurity job postings requiring AI skills doubled year over year across G7 countries, from 14.2% to 28.5%, according to an August 2026 analysis of recruitment data from Cornerstone and Indeed by the Cisco-founded AI Workforce Consortium. But it’s no longer enough for a cybersecurity professional to be technically strong. Candidates are also being screened for how they relate to the tools they use. “No company can afford to hire a new AI skeptic,” says LastPass’ Platt, adding that outright AI evangelism isn’t the goal either, because many of these capabilities haven’t been around long enough to prove themselves. “Assessing AI enthusiasm is key.” However, the appetite for AI-fluent hires runs ahead of what most organizations actually need right now, Fortium Partners’ Autrey cautions. Many clients ask his firm for AI security talent when what they most need is asset inventory, identity hygiene, data classification, and least-privilege capabilities. “AI did not invent a new control set,” he says. “It exposed the companies that never finished implementing and automating the old one.” Even when organizations try to validate AI competence, the tools they use may be lagging, too. Certifications are now the leading way organizations validate skills, ahead of degrees, says Lee of SANS Institute. “A certification is a timestamp,” he cautions. “It tells you when someone last proved it, not whether it is still true.” 5. A shrinking pipeline is becoming a security risk The same intelligent automation that’s driving cybersecurity role consolidation and boosting the importance of judgment is also closing off the paths cybersecurity pros traditionally took to develop their very human skills. Senior-titled cybersecurity postings grew 65% in the six months ending March 2026, while junior-titled postings grew just 5.9%, according to the AI Workforce Consortium . Autrey of Fortium Partners warns that Tier 1 SOC and manual control-testing work, long the apprenticeships for tomorrow’s senior analysts, are going unfilled when someone leaves . “If you automate the entry rung without replacing that learning path,” he says, “you are trading a cost reduction today for a talent shortage a few years from now.” The 2026 SANS/GIAC report confirms the pattern: the gap between the skills organizations need and the skills their teams actually have has widened from a four-percentage-point spread to 20 points in a single year, and AI is disrupting entry-level roles specifically. Skills gaps overtook headcount as organizations’ top workforce problem for the first time in 2025, according to the report, and the gap kept widening. Twenty-seven percent of organizations now tie an actual breach to a skills gap on their own team. “That is not a training request,” Lee of SANS Institute says. “That is an incident report with the training request stapled to the back.”

title: CW@60: A front-row seat – a journey through the tech startup scene across four countries
raw_text:
On 22 September 2026, Computer Weekly turns 60. To mark the milestone, we asked some of our friends - experts, parliamentarians, IT leaders and suppliers - for their perspectives on how tech has changed their lives over six decades. What's changed the most for you since then?

I didn’t study computer science, nor am I a tech bro or even technically minded for that matter, and yet somehow “tech” became my entire working life.

For a period, it even brought me into the Computer Weekly family as marketing director for a little over a year. Computer Weekly reaching its 60th anniversary is testament to its adaptability: from a printed, weekly magazine to now a key cog in a larger, digital machine - throughout which its influence has barely waned.

That evolution is something I relate to, closely mirroring my own in the media industry we share, one which has been disrupted possibly more than any other.

Australian beginnings

I grew up in Australia, and despite the university HTML classes I never attended and our introduction to the network protocol tool called Gopher, tech was far from my mind. Unsure what to do after my studies, I worked as a civil servant for a few years, and we had our own, proprietary (and rudimentary) version of email. But no internet, yet.

The event that would change this course landed serendipitously. I found a junior position selling advertising for the broadsheet newspaper, the Sydney Morning Herald, a venerated, 195-year-old institution. It was 2004 and salespeople were selling print classifieds to car yards and real estate agents, while a separate team would offer those same businesses a wonderful new “digital ad” as an add-on for free. In hindsight, it seems nuts. Although I recall we were puzzled in 2005 when the publisher of our magazine division left to join Google, curious why you’d ever leave such a prestigious institution.

Before long I was in tech media with Haymarket, a magazine publisher owned and operated by Michael Heseltine. In Australia, we published the gadget mag PC Authority, gamer and overclocking fanboy ‘zine Atomic MPC (Maximum Power Computing!), the industry rag Computer Reseller News and business coverage via IT News.

For the next six years, tech was everything I needed to know.

It was an intense period of speculation and discovery. Our British overlords sent a younger crew from headquarters to watch over the rowdy Australians. Many were just out of college and shared their lives with friends “back home” via Facebook following its launch there in late 2006.

We heard about the viral Twitter breakout at SXSW in March 2007 and I became an early user for both work and play, convincing many journalist colleagues to do the same.

The first iPod touch - the precursor of the iPhone - came into the office for editorial review in September 2007 and we all crowded around in utter amazement, taking turns to swipe here and there.

Nintendo sent some Wii games for review in late 2007, but no console. I called their PR and suggested that if they didn’t ship us one by the end of the week, Atomic MPC would review the box the game came in and its requisite cartridge.

I wrongly predicted that Microsoft’s Zune would take over from the iPod as it was a superior product - I maintain this latter point of view.

I didn’t buy a phone for many years. I’d just drop in on the gadget review team and walk away with something to replace the last one.

Media is a tough old business, and while Australia is a vast country it is also isolated. Tech media gave me the chance to see the rest of the world.

To London's Tech City

I moved to the UK in 2012 and while living with a startup founder in East London became immersed in the local startup community. It was the period of Silicon Roundabout, London’s Tech City, and Silicon Drinkabout. I looked out for cool startups to help on my weekends and spoke with many “blockchain for laundry” wantrepreneurs.

But I was also one of the early beta testers of Revolut. Having found them through Seedcamp, I even pitched them to help with marketing and met the only three members of the team in Level 39 in Canary Wharf.

I arrived at TechTarget as marketing director for Computer Weekly, among others, in February, 2015.

We took the new Women in Tech event from a few dozen people to a couple of hundred by aligning with London Tech Week and had it trending on Twitter - when that was still a big thing. A year later, we were planning Computer Weekly’s 50th anniversary celebrations. How time flies, eh? The poor editor Bryan Glick even had to traipse around London with me, looking for venues. 

French unicorns to US Midwest

I soon moved to France and jumped on its startup train, founding a marketing company called Iytro that provided part-time CMOs for early stage startups. We worked with some of the biggest and brightest in their field, many of whom have gone on to build unicorns and I sold it in 2023.

Now I find myself in the US, at a pivotal point in the story of what role tech plays in our lives. I am building my own tech media business called StartMidwest.

The heartland of the country has vast plains and huge, global historical companies, but tech growth on the coasts has seemingly passed it by. As re-industrialisation becomes a buzzword, robotics and AI are becoming deeply embedded in manufacturing and other essential industries. A nascent startup scene full of entrepreneurship and innovation aims to ensure the region fulfils its potential and keeps its best talent. We’re here to document it.

I’ve made my life working around tech - from machines and gadgets to the entrepreneurs changing our world, and I’ve done most of it from within the media industry. Tech has disrupted the world, and media has been one of the most disrupted of all industries.

I’m just glad to have had a front-row seat.

title: CW@60: Geek is good (eventually) – a social journey through technology
raw_text:
On 22 September 2026, Computer Weekly turns 60. To mark the milestone, we asked some of our friends - experts, parliamentarians, IT leaders and suppliers - for their perspectives on how tech has changed their lives over six decades. What's changed the most for you since then?

There is not enough space in a weighty book, let alone in one article, to detail all the incredible milestones that technology has achieved during the 60 years that Computer Weekly has been covering the sector.

There’s even more to come, of course. Even those 60 years will one day be looked back on as a time of mere baby steps in the digital revolution that continues to transform the way we live and work.

Artificial intelligence is the next accelerant. Quantum computing won’t be far behind. The advances in science and bioengineering and genetics and healthcare and robotics that will come in future will make the iPhone seem quaint.

I could pick many or any of the key tech developments of the past six decades as the one that impacted my digital lifetime and tell you a story about why. But that’s not the thing that, on reflection, stands out for me.

Not cool

One of the memorable moments of my first trip to India as a technology journalist in the early 2000s was sitting in a bar in Bangalore / Bengaluru with a couple of 20-something Indian lads – graduates from one of India’s excellent technology colleges - and listening to them tell me how working in IT helped them to meet girls. For young Indians, IT was cool.

This had not been my experience.

Like many in this trade, I was an accidental technology journalist. Many of us joke that nobody grew up wanting to be a “tech journo”. In fact, I was an accidental technologist even before that.

I ended up doing a computer science degree, simply because I thought it would be less boring than the maths degree I had originally signed up to. Sitting in a lecture theatre one day in my late teens, listening to a professor explaining the proof of why one is greater than zero, I realised there were some things in the world I was happy to accept as truth. One being greater than zero was one such fact.

Thanks to a common first year for the two courses, I switched to computer science, little realising I had set my path in reinforced concrete.

As a university student, my most common experience of studying tech came frequently. I’d be in a bar or at a party, chatting with people, making new friends, maybe even meeting a pleasant young lady. The conversation was going well. Laughter. Maybe a bit of flirtation. But all along I knew – eventually, the question would come.

“So, what do you study?”

“I’m doing computer science.”

“Oh…”

There endeth the conversation. Honestly – I can’t tell you how often that exact scenario played out. Computers were not cool.

Growth mode

In the late 1980s when I was job hunting, the UK IT sector was in growth mode. There were jobs aplenty – it was the obvious way to go for a computer science graduate. But I knew tech was not my long-term future, so I rejected the offers of programming roles and joined a trainee scheme that would lead to a job in sales. Learn to sell computers and I could sell anything, or so I hoped.

“In the 60 years of Computer Weekly, tech has gone from a dark and dull art, conducted in dingy basements, usually by middle-aged men with beards, to the most transformational and talked-about force on the planet”

Bryan Glick

Outside of work, the nineties were my dinner party years. Round a friend’s house, meeting new people, chatting before the food was served. Eventually, the question would come.

“So, what do you do?”

“I work in IT.”

“Oh…”

You never forget the look on someone’s face, when they realise their place at the dinner table for the next couple of hours was next to the geek who worked in IT.

Get those transferable skills in sales, go get a job in another sector that wasn’t as uncool as IT. That was the plan.

Gamekeeper turns poacher

Ten years later, after an only occasionally successful stint in selling IT, it turned out to be the sales skills I left behind as I switched careers and became a tech journalist. Gamekeeper turned poacher, writing about the flaws, frailties and failures of the industry in which I had previously worked.

Journalism is a sociable job – you meet lots of new people. And things took a turn for the better.

“So, what do you do?”

“I’m a journalist.”

“Really? That’s so interesting. What do you write about?”

“I write about technology.”

“Oh…”

Those extra few seconds of conversation before reaching the inevitable geek-alert moment were precious.

Of course, during much of the noughties, my goal was to develop my journalistic skills and move to a publication that didn’t write about tech. And of course, that didn’t happen. One look at my CV and all any recruiter saw was COMPUTERS.

Something big

Move forward another 10 years, by which time I was incredibly fortunate to be the editor in chief of Computer Weekly, with all the responsibility and career satisfaction that came from running the best-known brand in business technology publishing. And yes, things had changed.

“So, what do you do?”

“I’m a journalist.”

“Really? That’s so interesting. What do you write about?”

“I write about technology.”

“Ooh – which iPhone do you think I should buy?”

Well, it was an improvement. I at least got to reply, “I have no idea,” before the conversation began its downward drift. But it was the start of something big.

Another 10 years pass. It’s the 2020s. My joints ache more in the mornings, but I can enter the social side of the profession and even outside of work with a spring in my step. Why?

“So, what do you do?”

“I’m a journalist.”

“Really? That’s so interesting. What do you write about?”

“I write about technology.”

“Oh, wow – you must have so much to write about, there’s so much going in the tech world, isn’t there?”

And yes, dear reader - on occasions it has happened. My conversational partner would pause, and in that brief moment of silence unwittingly reveal the gravity – to me, at least - of what they were about to say.

“…That’s so cool.”

I knew it

Ladies and gentlemen – tech is cool. I *coughs* always knew it. And I’m so glad I stuck with it – and that it stuck with me.

In the 60 years of Computer Weekly – in my 60 years – tech has gone from a dark and dull art, conducted in dingy basements, usually by middle-aged men with beards, to the most transformational and talked-about force on the planet.

It was always that, of course – but perceptions matter. The perception of tech has changed, and in doing so it changed my life.

Geek is good.

title: CW@60: AI will change the economics of business more profoundly than the cloud
raw_text:
On 22 September 2026, Computer Weekly turns 60. To mark the milestone, we asked some of our friends - experts, parliamentarians, IT leaders and suppliers - for their perspectives on how tech has changed their lives over six decades. What's changed the most for you since then?

I have spent most of my working life watching technology change what it means to run a business.

When I started my career at Oracle in 1987, one of the assumptions that shaped business strategy was: the larger the company, the greater the advantage. This was especially true when it came to enterprise-grade software. It had to be installed, maintained, patched, upgraded, and integrated, which meant that it required resources that were often out of reach of smaller, growing businesses.

The cloud began to change that relationship by shifting much of the burden of running technology from the customer to the provider. As a result, a growing company could manage financials, inventory, customers, commerce, and reporting on the same kind of systems that had previously demanded much larger resources. Or put another way, a smaller company could operate with the sophistication, intelligence, and capacity once reserved for the world's largest enterprises without first becoming one.

This was a huge part of the opportunity we saw when we started NetSuite in 1998 - businesses should be able to use sophisticated software without having to own and operate all the infrastructure underneath it. As I look ahead, I believe what’s happening with artificial intelligence (AI) could have an even bigger impact on the economics of competition.

From the economics of technology to the economics of work

For decades, when a company expanded it became more complex, and the answer was usually to add capacity. More transactions meant more people. More markets meant more managers, systems, and coordination. More data meant larger analytics teams. Growth and organisational complexity tended to rise together. AI changes that equation.

In finance, for example, AI can help teams understand what is changing in the business before the month-end close. It can surface anomalies, identify patterns, and support forecasting without requiring the same level of manual analysis. A change in margin, cash flow, or revenue is rarely just a finance event. It can reflect changes in customer demand, pricing, inventory availability, production costs, or fulfillment performance. Connecting finance to the underlying operational reality is therefore critical to AI performance.

“The next generation of companies may have the reach, intelligence, control, and operating capacity of far larger organisations, while retaining the speed and agility of businesses a fraction of their size”

Evan Goldberg

AI can help companies interpret customer activity, manage inventory, forecast demand, and coordinate workflows. When these activities are connected in the same business system, AI can reason across them - linking a financial result to the orders, customers, supply, inventory, and operational decisions that produced it. That means companies can add new capabilities, enter new markets, or introduce new business models without growing their operations and costs at the same rate.

That changes the maths of growth. This is why I think AI will ultimately have a greater impact on the economics of running a business than the cloud. The cloud made enterprise technology more accessible. AI has the potential to do the same for enterprise capability.

The result may be a new kind of organisation - a company with the operational capabilities of a much larger business, but with the speed and agility of a smaller one.

AI still needs context

Stepping back, while AI changes many things, it does not eliminate the need for good business systems. In fact, it makes them more important.

The best AI still depends on the quality of the data and context it can access. It depends on having a connected, historical understanding of how a particular business operates. If data is incomplete, inconsistent, or disconnected, AI can only perform as well as the information available to it. A connected business suite gives AI a shared context across financials, customers, inventory, people, and workflows, allowing it to reason across the business rather than in isolated silos.

If AI is going to help operate a company, it needs reliable information about customers, orders, inventory, employees, revenue, and cash. It needs to understand how those records relate over time: which customers buy which products, what demand does to supply, how orders flow into revenue, and where operational decisions affect financial outcomes. It also needs to understand permissions, controls, and which actions people and technology are authorised to take. A trusted system of record becomes the foundation from which AI can reason, plan, and execute.

A different shape of company

Every major computing shift changes more than the technology itself. The PC changed who could access computing power. The internet changed how information moved. The cloud changed where computing happened and who could afford sophisticated business applications. Mobile changed how computing fit into daily life.

They also all have one other thing in common. Each of these eras began with the promise to level the playing field for smaller, growing organisations by democratising access to technology, but in the end the winners were “large” enterprises.

In contrast, the winners created by AI might not follow the traditional enterprise definition - thousands of employees, multiple layers of management, specialised departments, large budgets, complex systems - and instead just operate like them.

The next generation of companies may have the reach, intelligence, control, and operating capacity of far larger organisations, while retaining the speed and agility of businesses a fraction of their size.

The cloud allowed companies to use enterprise technology without first becoming enterprises. When grounded in a connected record of the whole business, AI can allow them to acquire enterprise capability without taking on enterprise complexity. Having watched the cloud reshape the technology industry, AI could reshape the economics of business itself.

Evan Goldberg is founder and executive vice president at Oracle NetSuite.
